Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
In article <766531d39...@anton.infoserv.com>, "Anton Dovydaitis"
<an...@infoserv.com> wrote:

> My thoughts on vote pushing. First, I think that V:TES is correct,
> that as many vote cards can be played by each Metheselah as are in
> their hands. This makes voting very dynamic, and Dark Sovereigns has
> increased this tendency with its variety of vote manipulating cards.
> In particular, Kindred Coercion: cancel or change the votes of X
> vampires younger than the reacting minion. This not only increases
> the uncertainty of votes generally, but diminishes weenie princes,
> whom I think are over-rated anyway. Another would be Conflict of
> Interest: cancel the votes of a vampire who belongs to the same clan
> as the reacting vampire. Both of these make votes more interesting
> and allow non-titled vampires to participate in politics to great effect.

Vote pushing is not effected by any of those cards.

> The only problem I've encountered in practice are the vote decks dominated
> by one or two vote cards (BORING), especially Kine Resources Contested.
> Anyway, it is my opinion that Dark Sovereigns mostly solves the political
> problem.

Now, on to vote push itself:

With vote pushing as the rules stand, both game dynamics are hurt and
deck construction is hurt.

A simple counterexample to allowing vote pushing is the Weenie Vote Push
deck. This deck is hugely destructive under 4CL and even more so in NL.
Unless specifically prepared for the damage even a 4CL Weenie Vote Push
deck can do, even NL decks can be swept off the table in spite of their
best efforts. Why? In the first turn minions act, WVP can have a prince
merely by throwing down X votes. In the next, they can throw down X-2
votes to win that turns votes. The 4CL WVP deck can easily have 8 votes
on the first vote, 10 votes on the second, and by the third turn, only
have to push occasionally. The rest is typically the downfall of the
table. The only other way for most decks to compete is to be able to
push as many votes as the WVP deck can. In a 4 player game, this means
an average of 2.666 votes per player. If they can't reliably get out 8
votes in the second turn, they can't compete. This kind of necessity
shuts down game dynamic.

Deck construction is tied to this. If one _must_ throw in enough
Political Actions to reliably get out your share of the votes early, your
choices become severely cramped. No deck should have to do this in case
another type of deck arrives. Strategies need to be accounted for (how
will I defend bleed? vote? combat?), but not specific necessities (I
_need_ 10% votes in my deck, I _need_ 10% X-type). Once one needs to
throw in the same certain cards in every deck to defend against that
strategy, you know you have a problem.

Deck construction is also hurt by the ease in which the vote deck can
cycle effortlessly. Got a useless vote (maybe a duplicate Praxis
Seizure), throw it in for one vote along with 6 others until you redraw
for you KRC/Sabbat Threat). Combat decks cannot just dump manuever after
manuever. Vote decks should have the same problem of hand jam as any
other deck.

With some (somewhat strict) form of vote push restriction, these problems
go away,

The WVP deck can no longer "insta-win". Instead, for an aggressive vote
deck to win, it must figure out ways to keep the aggressive votes in hand
_and_ have political power on the board.

Other players are no longer forced to have turn 2 defense or else. They
can choose to handle vote defense in any number of ways.

Vote decks are brought to an equal status with every other deck: They
must work to get cards out of their hands.

Oftentimes, people respond by saying that Methuselahs, being ancient
vampires of power and influence, have some kind of innate control over
politics. What is missed by this idea is that there are _many_
Methuselahs, and the players at the table only represent _some_ of these
Methuselahs. As one of many, these Methuselahs do have some impact, but
that other Methuselahs' ambitions are thrown into the mix as well. Maybe
an unnamed Methuselah doesn't want it to happen. As a result, the
Methuselah's actual physical influence is typically very small. They
only influence Camarilla politics through the actually people involved in
them that they control. As an aside, since many vampires doubt the
existence of Methuselahs, why should they change their vote because there
are rumors that a Methuselah wants something done and another Methuselah
disagrees.

As always, I welcome any commentary...

Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
Jonathan G. Sushinsky <jona...@cesar.umd.edu> wrote:
>I have mentioned before that I personally do not see a problem with vote
>pushing. The Weenie Vote Deck counter to that just does not seem to be a
>good enough reason to disallow vote pushing. It may seem kind of wierd
>when you see Nik becoming the Prince of Houston on the second round and
>all, but I don't think that this is that much of a threat. so what if
>the WVD gets 2 new vampires out every turn. Voting is a one stealth deal
>(in general). All the prey of the WVD has to do is intercept the
>important ones (KRC's CA's etc...), and most decks should have some
>limited intecept skill.

Ok. Let's look at this differently.

"What if a player was playing a deck using all size 1-3 vampires, each of whom
could bleed at 3 or 4 each turn? Heck, bleeding actions are at ZERO stealth,
anyone can block that. Who cares if he can get out two more vamps each turn?"

A harmful vote is the same as a large bleed that starts with plus one stealth,
that any schmuckola wimp of a Nik can do.

Ideally, this should be balanced by the fact that it's a vote, and people could
use politics to stop it. However, the fact that the player who call the vote
can drop a handful of cards every time to support it eliminates this balancing
factor.

On the other hand, if the vote pushing is restricted, the player can't simply
load up his deck with dual purpose political action cards. If he wants his
votes passed, he'll have to resort to all those neato vote fiddling cards.
Suddenly, he's got to make the same deck design choices as everyone else. How
many PA cards to put in, vs how many vote modifier cards so that they'll
actually pass?

Messages.Author: Jonathan G. Sushinsky
Messages.Body:
I have mentioned before that I personally do not see a problem with vote
pushing. The Weenie Vote Deck counter to that just does not seem to be a
good enough reason to disallow vote pushing. It may seem kind of wierd
when you see Nik becoming the Prince of Houston on the second round and
all, but I don't think that this is that much of a threat. so what if
the WVD gets 2 new vampires out every turn. Voting is a one stealth deal
(in general). All the prey of the WVD has to do is intercept the
important ones (KRC's CA's etc...), and most decks should have some

limited intecept skill. All the predator need's to do is get an action
blocked. Anytime a weenie gets into combat _anyone_ should be able to
put them in torpor. So 1 intercepted vote and doing one thing to make
the weenies block per turn will negate the fact that they are getting a
couple of new (titleless) vampires out. Soon they have more princes in
torpor than they do ready vampires and that hardly seems to be too
threatening.

If you would like me to mail you the WVP Deck, try it out for yourself.
Ask your friends if you can use proxies, and don't substitute for any
other cards. The rules: Just don't tell your friends what you are
playing. I.e., the game should _begin_ with natural prey/predator
relationships.

Your ideas:
Nik becoming a prince not a threat:
It allows the WVP deck to have to push less votes. On the second
turn, unless one can reliably supply 8 votes, Nik will be prince. Also
highly likely is that their will be 2 princes on turn 2.

So what about en masse:
Calling offensive votes each turn will be blockable (+1 intercept
needed), and blocking one should destroy (or nearly so) the caller. So
what? For 1 more pool, I can bring him back out, and drop contesting the
weak one. Meanwhile, 2 to 5+ offensive votes can be called, and if they
aren't called, more princes are coming out. By this time, the WVP deck
couldn't care if Half its vampires died in the next turn.

The vote deck will block:
It shouldn't. Take the bleed, even if it is a conditioning on
Govern teh Unaligned. By the time they are able to consistently hurt
you, you have likely finished off a prey or two.

Intercept the important votes:
Which ones? Even in 4CL, thats 24 votes, plus the 8 others that
are damaging in round about ways (First Tradition, etc...) And how many
minions do _you_ have to block them all.

Things you forgot to mention:
Bum's Rush decks:
Can't take out enough of em. Swarm effect.

Problems for the WVP:
Contesting another WVP. Playing another VP. Justine with a Sport
Bike. Other than that, there is not much likelihood of loosing.

From a game standpoint, why should politics get special treatment? Every
other deck has to work to get the appropriate cards in hand, not just
drop them in a de facto Deal with the Devil. Without VP, the WVP deck
can be made, but it must have contingencies for how to pass early votes.
It must begin to make choices like "How many votes? How many
reactions/modifiers?" It becomes an excercise in deck _design_, not a
no-brainer,

Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
Jonathan G. Sushinsky <jona...@cesar.umd.edu> wrote:

>Then this is exacly the vote that should be targeted for intercept.
>Chooseing when and what to block becomes the strategy involved. Most of
>us love strategical challenges (I would think that is why most of us
>would rather play Jyhad than M:tg) and in my opinion restricting vote
>pushing eliminates a very strategic portion of the game.
>
>Choosing your battles is a very important concept of playing the game
>well IMO.Relating this to your big bleed argument. if you only have two
>blocking minions and your predator has four vampires to bleed with you
>had better block the malks with DOM rather than worrying about the two
>who have a laptop who can only bleed for 2.

The problem being that a WVP deck has very few political actions that are NOT
dangerous. I'm not going have have my horde of weenies calling "Regaining the
Upper Hand". They're going to be calling one of the damaging votes (plus
Autarkus Persecution - if you can call me gaining 5-6 more pool than everyone
else not dangerous). And they're going to be a lot of them calling these
votes.

The bleed defense comparison breaks down here, because any caitiff can call a
5 point CA vote - but the smallest vamp with Sup. Dom. is a 4. So, of the four
Caitiffs I brought out at the same time as your 4pt Malk, you block a couple of
their damage votes, the other two get passed, whammo, 6-8 pool gone. Oh, and
unless you're an Auspex player, you aren't even blocking those, because the
permanent based intercept is comparatively slow to get out.

As you stated, one has to make choices when defending against a bleed, too.
Fine. This is a strategic game. But let's look at what you're up against,
before you even get to make a defensive choice :

A bleed action : zero stealth. 1 Damage. Can be modified upwards for big
vamps, or by equip actions down stream. Can be intercepted.

A vote action : 1 stealth. micro vamps do as much damage as a big vamp does
bleeding. Always passes under Vote Push. Can be intercepted.

The defense against both is the same - intercept. However, votes come with
extra stealth. Votes are being played by smaller, and thus more numerous
vampires. Ergo, votes are much harder to defend against, on a per-unit damage
basis.

So, of the two fundamental ways of hurting your opponent that exist in the
game, one is clearly more effective than the other. There's something wrong.
If you restrict Vote Push, then it evens out. While the bleeder has to have
bigger vamps and play extra cards to get plus bleed, the voter has to have
bigger vamps (for titles/presence), play cards, and finagle to get his vote
passed.

We all like to choose our battles, and make strategic choices. But for weenie
vote push, there are no choices. Vamp after vamp plays the same class of
cards, discarding happily to pass it if he's not blocked. If he's blocked, the
next vamp in line tries the same thing. Repeat until not blocked. Yawn.

They *all* call KRC (or have a bleed of 3) - you can't choose a better
time to block because all the actions are the same. You block the
first two or the last two - it won't matter. The other two get
though and you lose 6 pool. (Typically there are more than four
vampires - usu. 5 or 6 - so you'll be losing 9 or 12 pool each turn
you block only two - even when you block the best two).

Yes, choosing your battles is a key concept in a non-degenerate game.
Vote-push makes a degenerate game possible - and choosing your
battles is a meaningless concept in that case.

I agree that it should never be a no-brainer, defending should also get
this type of attention though. If you rule out vote pushing, defenses
against vote decks become much simpler and it is easy to pack a few Dread
Gazes rather than worry about how many votes might be thrown in each
turn.

effectively know if a PA is going to pass or fail-based on what is
already on the table. This makes a very important aspect of the game
rather dry and meaningless (to use yet another contoversial phrase :)

In any case carry on. Our differing beliefs are not likely to persuade

fall off, but I probably will lurk back into the shadows of the
discussion for awhile and let someone else take up the "vote pushing is
an essential part of the game" debate for a while. I'll jump back in
after doing some experiments with your deck, but don't hold your breath
waiting :).

Messages.Author: Shane Travis
Messages.Body:
Simon Richardson (si...@onechip.co.uk) wrote:

: Also don't forget that the bloodhunt vote that follows the destruction of a

: weenie prince does not permit vote pushing. It's done using old-fashioned
: "count the vampires" method.

While you may play this as a house rule, this is not actually the case.

In a Bloodhunt, anyone may play Political Action cards to gain additional
vots, at 1 per PA. Also, titled vampires may use their titles to vote.
Finally, the Ventrue Headquarters may be tapped for 3 additional votes.

There are no votes given for merely 'existing': votes in a bloodhunt may
only be gained in one of the above three ways.

Action Modifiers and Reaction cards which add/manipulate votes may _not_
be used during a Bloodhunt.

Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
Robert Rodger <robert...@earthlink.net> wrote:
>
>I don't understand what you mean that he'll "suddenly have to make the
>same deck design choices as every one else". No first off, I'm not
>entirely certain what is meant by a Weenie Vote Deck, but I play a
>Ventrue vote deck, and have been working hard on tuning it and getting a
>good balance: votes to do damage (it's my primary weapon), blockers to
>avoid getting hit by too many bleeds, and some vamps with Obfuscate to
>call the tricky votes which the combat decks could intercept and ruin.

Great! IMHO, that's what a vote deck should be. I'm not griping at that.

Someone else just posted deck designs for WVP under both NL and 4CL.

But the gist of it is :

lots of votes to do damage.
lots of small vampires.

....and that's it!

This deck doesn't need to worry about combat defense. Just bring out another
vampire!

It doesn't need to worry about passing the vote - just burn your whole hand for
a bunch more votes!

This deck doesn't worry about bleed defense. It can kill its prey faster than
you can bleed it.

This deck doesn't need to worry about stealth - votes come with stealth
already, and with so many small vampires, you won't be able to intercept all
the votes.

>And yes, unlike Magic, Jyhad is a strategy game. If my oponant can't
>figure out when to block one of my votes and when not to waste the
>effort, then I guess he's technically as good a player.

There are no votes in a "weenie vote push" deck that are safe to let pass.

FWIW, here's the comparison between a Vote action to damage and a Bleed
action. These two actions are the two most direct ways to damage your prey,
which is what the game's all about :

Bleed: 0 stealth. Does 1 damage. More damage with larger vamps (and plus
bleed cards) and equipment.

Vote : 1 stealth. Does 3-4 damage. Vamp size irrelevant. Can be voted down.

The problem - if you allow people to discard whole hands of PA cards to get
extra votes, the last limitation of a Vote - "can be voted down" - becomes
irrelevant, making voting clearly better than bleeding.
